title: Noise, Direction, and the Cost of Experiments

articles.title: Discovering a scaling law has its own compute budget
articles.paper: SLDBench v2: Active Scaling Law Discovery

blocks.title: Background
blocks.text: Chinchilla (2022) used small-scale training runs to study compute allocation between model size and data. SLDBench (2025; ICLR 2026) then asked agents to discover predictive laws automatically. The new question: obtaining the fitting data itself costs compute.[6,7]
The expression above is only a candidate form. The agent neither knows the correct functional form nor gets all observations for free; it receives a catalog of priced experiments.[5]

\(x_i\) is a training configuration; \(c_i\) is usually its training FLOPs. The outcome \(y_i\) is revealed only after purchase. Omitting group indices, the agent buys \(A_t\) each round and stops at time \(\tau\):

Evaluation records \((\text{extrapolation error at larger scales},\,\rho)\). The agent must jointly decide **which experiments to buy, when to stop, and which law to fit**. Test configurations are larger than candidate experiments and cannot be purchased directly.[5]

blocks.caption: 30 selected difficult tasks and 8 agent systems. The R² range is across systems, not a confidence interval.[5]

blocks.title: What to take away
blocks.text: Cheap experiments may cover every group while losing the independent parameter variation needed to identify the law. Experimental design adds a bottleneck to automated scaling-law discovery; these results concern the selected difficult tasks.[5]

classic.question: If long memory depends on the full kernel Kⱼ = CĀʲB̄, is moving the eigenvalues of Ā toward the unit circle enough? How do input/output directions and non-normality affect memory?

blocks.title: Where it comes from
blocks.text: Long sequences require both memory and efficient training. HiPPO (2020) designed continuous memory through polynomial projections; S4 (2022) sought a state-space parameterization that is fast to compute and numerically stable.[10,13]

Consider one channel with scalar input and output, and hidden state \(x(t)\in\mathbb R^N\). \(A\) governs memory evolution, \(B\) writes the input, and \(C\) reads the state. Omit the separately computable skip term.[12]
Apply a bilinear discretization with step size \(\Delta>0\), assuming the inverse exists. \(\Delta\) is the sampling timescale and can be learned as a model parameter.[12]
With zero initial state \(x_{-1}=0\) and fixed parameters, stepwise recurrence and full-sequence convolution are exactly equivalent:[12]

blocks.label: RNN ↔ convolution
blocks.tex: \begin{aligned}x_k&=\bar A x_{k-1}+\bar B u_k,\\ y_k&=\sum_{j=0}^{k}K_j u_{k-j},\qquad K_j=C\bar A^j\bar B.\end{aligned}

blocks.title: Two execution modes for the same layer
blocks.text: Use convolution to process the full sequence in parallel during training; retain only the current state during autoregressive generation. Linearity applies to the individual SSM kernel. Channel mixing and nonlinearities between layers give the full network nonlinear expressive power.[10,12]

**Computing the kernel is the real bottleneck.** Direct eigendecomposition of a HiPPO matrix can be severely ill-conditioned. S4 uses a normal matrix plus a low-rank correction, then a unitary change of basis gives DPLR:[10]

blocks.label: Structured parameterization
blocks.tex: A=V(\Lambda-PQ^*)V^*,\qquad V^*V=I,\qquad P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r},\quad r\ll N.

blocks.text: \(\Lambda\) is diagonal. Write \(\widehat A=\Lambda-PQ^*\) and \(R(\omega)=(\omega I-\Lambda)^{-1}\). When the relevant inverses exist, Woodbury’s identity gives:[10]

A high-dimensional inverse becomes a diagonal inverse plus an \(r\times r\) correction. The paper reduces the finite-length kernel’s generating function to Cauchy computations and an inverse FFT. For fixed low rank, theoretical kernel construction costs \(\widetilde O(N+L)\), and each recurrent step costs \(O(N)\). These are per-SSM costs and assume a fast Cauchy algorithm.[10]

blocks.title: Discussion · our interpretation
blocks.text: \(K_j=C\bar A^j\bar B\) suggests that long memory depends on both dynamics and input–output coupling. Is placing eigenvalues near the unit circle enough? For non-normal \(\bar A\), which transient effects does the spectral radius miss? These are questions for further discussion, not conclusions proved by the paper.
